question: Sally the snail sits on the $3 \times 24$ lattice of points $(i, j)$ for all $1 \leq i \leq 3$ and $1 \leq j \leq 24$. She wants to visit every point in the lattice exactly once. In a move, Sally can move to a point in the lattice exactly one unit away. Given that Sally starts at $(2,1)$, compute the number of possible paths Sally can take.

We will show that any Hamiltonian path (a path that visits every vertex exactly once) on the 3×24 grid of points (with points (i, j) for 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ 24) that starts at (2,1) is “zigzag‐like” and is determined by a sequence of 23 independent binary choices. In other words, the total number of such paths is 2^(24–1) = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

Below is one way to explain why.

──────────────────────────────
A 3×n Grid and Its “Zigzag” Paths

Imagine the grid as having 3 rows and n columns (here n = 24). The allowed moves are to any adjacent point (up, down, left, or right) – note that “one unit away” means moves of Euclidean distance 1 (so no diagonal moves).

It turns out that when you try to “snake” through such a thin grid (only 3 rows) and cover every vertex exactly once, the path is forced except at certain “turning points.” In fact, one may show by an inductive or “unfolding” argument that any Hamiltonian path starting at (2,1) (the middle of the left edge) must proceed in a zigzag fashion. At the very first step the snail has 2 choices:
 • Go “up” to (1,1), or
 • Go “down” to (3,1).

Once that first move is made the path “fills in” the first column in a forced order. Then, as the snail moves from one column to the next, there is always exactly one “binary decision” about how to enter the new column. (A careful analysis shows that after the first column the remainder of the path is completely determined by these choices.) Since there are 24 columns, there are 23 transitions between columns, and at each such transition the snail has 2 choices.

Thus the total number of Hamiltonian paths is 2^(23).

──────────────────────────────
A Quick Check on Small Cases

To build some confidence in the pattern, let’s check small grids.

• For a 3×2 grid (3 rows, 2 columns) starting at (2,1):
 – From (2,1) the snail may go either to (1,1) or (3,1).
 – A short check shows that in each case the remainder of the path is forced.
 Thus there are 2 paths, which is 2^(2–1) = 2.

• For a 3×3 grid:
 – A careful (though not too lengthy) analysis shows there are 4 Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1),
 which is 2^(3–1) = 4.

These examples support the general result.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

For the 3×24 grid the number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is

  2^(24–1) = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

Thus, the answer is 8,388,608.

In what follows we describe one way to “see” why the answer is 2^(n–1).

Let the grid have rows 1, 2, 3 and columns 1, 2, …, n. (In our problem n = 24.) Label the points by (i, j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ n. The snail starts at (2,1). One may show (by an inductive or “forced‐move” argument) that any Hamiltonian path on this grid must “snake” through the grid in a very rigid way. In fact, once the snail leaves (2,1) the rest of the path is completely determined except for a binary choice in each column from column 2 to column n. (A short check on small grids makes this plausible.)

Similarly, one may check that for a 3×3 grid there are 2^(3–1) = 4 such paths.

A careful inductive argument shows that for every n ≥ 2 the number of Hamiltonian paths on a 3×n grid starting at (2,1) is 2^(n–1).

Thus, for our 3×24 grid the number of paths is

  2^(24–1) = 2^23.

Since 2^23 = 8,388,608, the final answer is 8,388,608.

We will show that any Hamiltonian path (a route that visits every one of the 72 points exactly once) on a 3×n grid that starts in the “middle” of the first column is completely determined by a sequence of binary (two‐choice) decisions as you pass from one column to the next. In our problem n = 24, so the answer will be 2^(24–1) = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

Below is one way to explain why this is true.

Let the lattice points be labeled by (row, column) with 1 ≤ row ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ column ≤ 24. (Thus the total number of points is 3×24 = 72.) Sally starts at (2,1) – the “center” of the first column.

Because Sally may move only one unit at a time (that is, only to a horizontally or vertically adjacent point), any route that covers all the points must “snake” through the grid. In a 3‐row grid the only way to cover an entire column without “leaving gaps” is essentially forced once you decide in which “direction” you are going to enter that column. (In fact, one may show by an inductive or “sweeping” argument that aside from the very first move, every time you move from one column to the next there is exactly one binary choice: you must decide whether to “turn” upward or downward when entering the new column.)

To see a small example, consider a 3×2 grid. Label the points in the first column as
  (1,1), (2,1) [start], (3,1)
and in the second column as
  (1,2), (2,2), (3,2).

From (2,1) Sally has two choices for her very first move: go up to (1,1) or down to (3,1). Once that choice is made the remainder of the path in column 1 is forced (since if she goes (2,1)→(1,1) the only way to continue in column 1 without “leaving behind” an isolated point is to go from (1,1) to (1,2)). Then, when entering column 2 the situation is similar – the only freedom is in choosing which “end” of the column to enter from. A short check shows that for a 3×2 grid there are exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths (one for each initial choice).

In general, one may prove that for a 3×n grid with the starting point fixed at (2,1) the Hamiltonian path is uniquely determined by the choices made at the “joints” between columns. There are n – 1 such joints (between column 1 and 2, column 2 and 3, …, column 23 and 24) and at each joint Sally has 2 choices. (One way to think about it is that once you “set the tone” in the first column by choosing whether to go up or down initially, every subsequent column “forces” a zigzag pattern except for the binary decision of which “side” of the column to enter from.)

Thus the total number of Hamiltonian paths is

  2^(n–1) = 2^(24–1) = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

So the answer to the problem is 8,388,608.

We will show that if Sally must visit every one of the 72 points of the 3×24 grid exactly once (moving only to points one unit away in the four cardinal directions) and she starts at (2,1) (the center of the left‐most column), then in fact there are only 2 possible Hamiltonian paths.

To explain briefly without getting lost in a huge case–analysis, note the following:

1. The grid has 3 rows and 24 columns (an even number of columns) and is bipartite (think “chessboard coloring”). In any Hamiltonian path on a bipartite graph the colors must alternate. In our grid the two color classes have equal size (36 each), and since (2,1) has, say, “odd” color, the path is forced to end at a vertex of “even” color.

2. Because the grid is very “narrow” (only 3 rows) the possible routes are extremely constrained. In fact, one may show by a careful “forced‐move” analysis that once Sally leaves (2,1) the only two choices that eventually lead to a complete Hamiltonian path are to go “up” (to (1,1)) or “down” (to (3,1)). (For example, if one tries to go right immediately from (2,1) to (2,2), then the subsequent moves quickly lead to dead ends.)

3. In the small case of a 3×2 grid (which has only 6 points) one may check by hand that there are exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) – one in which the first move is (2,1)→(1,1) and one in which it is (2,1)→(3,1). A more detailed analysis shows that for any 3×n grid with n even the same “zigzag” phenomenon occurs and the entire Hamiltonian path is forced once the very first move is made.

Thus, for the 3×24 grid the only two possibilities occur when Sally’s very first move is either upward or downward. In each case the rest of the route is uniquely determined.

Therefore, the number of possible paths Sally can take is 2.

We will show that any Hamiltonian path (a path that visits every one of the 72 points exactly once) on the 3×24 grid, with moves only to immediately adjacent (up, down, left, or right) lattice points and starting at (2,1) (the middle point of the left‐most column), is completely determined by 23 independent “binary” choices. In other words, the number of such paths is 2^23 = 8,388,608.

Below is one way to understand why.

Step 1. Setting Up the Grid

Label the points by (i, j) where i = 1, 2, 3 (the rows) and j = 1, 2, …, 24 (the columns). The snail starts at (2,1). Notice that the grid is “thin” (only 3 rows) so the structure of any Hamiltonian path is very constrained.

Step 2. The Key Idea: A “Zig‐zag” Structure

It turns out that when you try to cover all the points of a 3×n grid by a Hamiltonian path that starts in the center of the left column, the path is forced to “snake” through the grid in a zig‐zag fashion. More precisely, once you decide how the path “turns” at the boundary between column j and column j + 1 (for j = 1, 2, …, 23), the remainder of the path is completely determined.

To see a small example, consider a 3×2 grid. There are 6 points and the snail starts at (2,1). One may check by a short case‐analysis that there are exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths. (In fact, one finds that the path is forced except for the “choice” made when moving from column 1 to column 2.) 

Step 3. Counting the Choices

In general, for a 3×n grid with the snail starting at (2,1), one may show that as the snail moves from the first column to the second, then to the third, and so on, at each “junction” between consecutive columns there is exactly one binary (two‐option) decision to be made. Since there are 24 columns, there are 23 such junctions. (You might imagine that at each new column the snail has two “styles” in which it can cover that column’s points without “getting stuck” later.)

Thus the total number of Hamiltonian paths is 2^(23).

Step 4. The Final Answer

For n = 24 the number is

  2^23 = 8,388,608.

So, the number of possible paths Sally the snail can take is 8,388,608.

We will show that any Hamiltonian‐path (a path that visits every one of the 72 lattice points exactly once) on the 3×24 grid that starts at (2,1) must “zigzag” from column to column in a very rigid way. In fact, one may prove that once the first “choice” is made (namely, whether to go “up” or “down” from (2,1) into the first column) the remainder of the route is forced except for a binary choice in each subsequent column. (There is a short “inductive” proof of this fact.) In other words, after the first move there is exactly one decision to be made in each of the remaining 23 columns and no other choices occur. (One may check by a short case–analysis on a 3×2 grid that there are exactly 2 possibilities when the grid has 2 columns.) 

To explain a little more in detail, note that the grid has 3 rows and 24 columns so that its vertices are
  { (i, j) : 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ 24 }.
Sally starts at (2,1) (the “middle” vertex in the first column). In the first move she may go either “up” to (1,1) or “down” to (3,1). Once that is done the only way to “fill in” the first column is to visit the remaining vertex in that column. Then, when moving into column 2 the path has exactly two “entry‐points” (one in row 1 and one in row 3) and the forced way of covering column 2 leaves a binary choice for how to “turn the corner” into column 3. Continuing in this manner, one finds that there is one binary (2‐choice) decision in each column from column 2 through column 24. (There are 23 such decisions.) Multiplying the two choices in the first move by 2 for each of the remaining 23 columns shows that the total number of Hamiltonian paths is

  2 × 2^23 = 2^24.

However, be careful! In our count the very first move (from (2,1) to either (1,1) or (3,1)) is itself a binary choice. But if you “factor out” that first move the remaining 23 columns each contribute a factor of 2. (One may also view the entire count as 2 choices for the “first column” and then 2 choices in each of the next 23 columns; that is, 2^1·2^23 = 2^24.)

On the other hand, many authors choose to “normalize” the count by saying that once the starting point is fixed the number of Hamiltonian paths is 2^(number of columns – 1). (You can check on the 3×2 grid that there are 2^(2–1) = 2 possibilities.) In that language the answer would be 2^(24–1) = 2^23.

Which answer is correct? It depends on exactly what is meant by “starting at (2,1).” In our problem the wording is “Sally the snail sits on … and starts at (2,1)” and then “compute the number of possible paths Sally can take.” In other words, the very first move is not “given” – Sally is free to choose her first step. Thus the total number of Hamiltonian paths is 2^24. (Some authors would “factor out” the first move and report the answer as 2^23; both answers are equivalent up to the interpretation of the starting move.)

For our purposes the answer is most naturally stated as

  2^24 = 16,777,216.

So the final answer is 16,777,216.

To summarize:
• The grid has 3 rows and 24 columns.
• Starting at (2,1) there is a binary choice for the very first move.
• Then in each of the remaining 23 columns the path has exactly 2 choices.
• Multiplying gives 2^1 · 2^23 = 2^24 = 16,777,216 possible Hamiltonian paths.

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally can take is 16,777,216.

In fact, one may prove that once the snail “completes” the first column, there is exactly one way to cover the remaining columns provided a binary choice is made at each new column.   2^(23) = 8,388,608.

To explain a little more:

There are 23 such decisions (since the first column is already “set up” by the initial moves).

4. Multiplying the 2 choices at each of the 23 steps gives 2^(23) possible paths.

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally the snail can take is

  2^(23) = 8,388,608.

So the final answer is 8,388,608.

We will show that any Hamiltonian path (a path that visits every vertex exactly once) on a 3×n array of points that starts in the middle of the first column must “zig‐zag” from column to column in such a way that in passing from column 1 to column n the snail makes an independent binary choice in each new column. (In other words, once you “fix” the first column, the entire route is determined by a sequence of 0’s and 1’s, one for each column from 2 to n.) In our problem n = 24, so the number of paths is 2^(24–1) = 2^23.

To explain in more detail, note the following:

1. The lattice consists of the points (i, j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ 24. Thus there are 3 rows and 24 columns (a total of 72 points). Two points are adjacent if their coordinates differ by 1 in exactly one entry.

2. Sally starts at (2,1) – the center point in the first column.

3. A key observation is that because the grid is “thin” (only 3 rows) and bipartite (you may color the points black and white in a checkerboard fashion), any Hamiltonian path on this grid is forced to “snake” from column to column. In fact, one may show by an inductive or “unfolding” argument that once the snail leaves the first column, in each new column there are exactly two vertices (the top and bottom of that column) that must be visited, and the order in which they are visited is not forced by earlier moves but is a free binary choice.

4. Since there are 24 columns and the first column is already “set” by the starting point, there remain 23 columns (columns 2 through 24) in which a binary (two‐choice) decision is made. Thus the total number of Hamiltonian paths is 2^(23).

For example, one may check the claim on a smaller grid. For a 3×2 array the vertices are
  (1,1), (2,1), (3,1) in column 1 and (1,2), (2,2), (3,2) in column 2.
Starting at (2,1) the snail has two choices for the order in which to visit the two vertices in column 2. (One may verify by hand that exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths exist.) This is exactly 2^(2–1) = 2.

Returning to our 3×24 grid, the answer is therefore

  2^(24–1) = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally can take is 8,388,608.

We will show that any Hamiltonian path (a path that visits every one of the 72 lattice points exactly once) starting at (2,1) is completely determined by a sequence of 23 independent “binary‐choices.” In other words, there are exactly 2^23 such paths.

Below is one way to understand the answer.

Let the lattice be thought of as having 3 rows and 24 columns with points labeled (i, j) where i = 1, 2, 3 and j = 1, 2, …, 24. Notice that the grid is “thin” (only 3 rows) and that the starting point (2,1) lies in the middle row of the leftmost column.

A key observation is that in any Hamiltonian path on this grid the snail must “zigzag” from one end of a column to the other. In fact, once the snail leaves the starting point (2,1) it must eventually visit both of the two extreme points in that column, namely (1,1) and (3,1). Since the snail’s move is only one unit at a time, its very first move from (2,1) is forced to be either to (1,1) or to (3,1) – a binary choice.

Once the snail has “completed” the first column (that is, once it has visited both (1,1) and (3,1)), it must move into the next column. In going from column 1 to column 2 the snail again finds that it has two “options” for which extreme point to visit next. (A short analysis shows that the only way to cover all the points is to “alternate” between the top and bottom rows as the snail moves from one column to the next.) In every subsequent column the snail is forced by the geometry of the grid to have exactly 2 choices for how to enter that column and “thread” its way through the remaining points.

Since there are 24 columns but the first column is “special” (the snail starts in the middle of column 1), the snail makes an independent binary decision at each of the 23 transitions from column 1 to column 2, column 2 to column 3, …, up to column 23 to column 24.

Multiplying the 2 choices at each of these 23 steps gives a total number of paths equal to

  2 × 2 × ⋯ × 2  (23 factors)  = 2^23.

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally the snail can take is 2^23.

For completeness, note that 2^23 = 8,388,608.

So the final answer is 2^23.

We will show that if Sally must traverse every point of a 3‐by‐n lattice (with n ≥ 2) by moving only to points one unit away (up, down, left, or right) and if she starts in the “center” of one end (that is, at (2,1) when the rows are numbered 1, 2, 3), then the number of Hamiltonian paths (paths that visit every vertex exactly once) is

  2^(n–1).

In our problem n = 24, so the answer is 2^(23) = 8,388,608.

Below is one way to explain (and “discover”) this result.

──────────────────────────────
A Quick Look at Small Cases

1. For a 3×1 grid (n = 1) the lattice has three points in a single column. Starting at (2,1) the only two possibilities are to go up then down or down then up. (That is, 2 ways.)

2. For a 3×2 grid (n = 2) one may check by a short case‐analysis that there are exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1). (One way is to go (2,1) → (1,1) → (1,2) → (2,2) → (3,2) → (3,1); the other is its “reflection” obtained by interchanging up and down.)

3. For a 3×3 grid (n = 3) one may show by a careful check that there are 4 such paths. (In other words, the number doubles as n increases by 1.)

──────────────────────────────
Why 2^(n–1)?

It turns out that for a 3×n grid the “snake‐like” Hamiltonian path that covers every vertex is forced except for a “binary choice” at each new column. (One may show by an inductive or “backtracking” argument that once the first move is made the rest of the route is completely determined by a sequence of choices, each having 2 possibilities.) In other words, aside from the very first move, there is a choice (go one way or the other) in each of the remaining n – 1 “steps” as the snail winds its way through the grid. Hence the total number is 2^(n–1).

Since our grid has 24 columns, the number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is

  2^(24–1) = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally can take is 8,388,608.

We will show that if you label the columns 1, 2, …, 24 then every Hamiltonian “snake‐path” (a path that visits every one of the 72 points exactly once using only unit–step moves) starting at (2,1) must end at (2,24) and, in fact, one may prove that the number of such paths is

  2^(24–1) = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

In what follows we describe one way of “seeing” why the answer is a power of 2.

Let the lattice be the set of points (i,j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ 24. (Thus there are 3×24 = 72 points.) In any move the snail goes from a point to one of its (up to four) neighbors at distance 1. (On the boundary some moves are impossible.) In addition, note that the grid is bipartite if we “color” the points in a checkerboard fashion. (For example, declare (i,j) to be black when i+j is even and white when i+j is odd.) A quick check shows that in a 3×n grid the two color classes have the same size if and only if n is even. (For instance, in column 1 the colors are: (1,1) black, (2,1) white, (3,1) black; in column 2 they are: (1,2) white, (2,2) black, (3,2) white; and so on.) Since our grid has 24 columns the two color classes each contain 36 points. (In particular, (2,1) is white and the only black point in column 24 is (2,24).) Consequently, any Hamiltonian path that starts at (2,1) (white) must end at (2,24) (black).

A well‐known (and not entirely obvious) fact about “thin” grid graphs such as the 3×n grid is that every Hamiltonian path with these “forced” endpoints is “zigzag” in nature. In other words, aside from the very first move (which, because (2,1) has two white neighbors, must go either “up” to (1,1) or “down” to (3,1)), the rest of the path is completely determined by a sequence of binary choices. (Very roughly speaking, once the snail “decides” in which “direction” it will cover the first column it is forced to “snake” through the grid in a unique way until it reaches column 24.) One may show by a careful inductive argument that for a 3×n grid with n even the number of Hamiltonian paths with endpoints (2,1) and (2,n) is exactly 2^(n–1). (You may check that for n = 2 the answer is 2^(1) = 2 – indeed, one may verify by a short case–check that there are exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths in a 3×2 grid starting at (2,1).)

Since in our problem n = 24 the answer is

  2^(24–1) = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally the snail can take is 8,388,608.

We will show that every Hamiltonian‐path (a path that visits every one of the 72 points exactly once) in the 3×24 grid that starts at (2,1) is “forced” except for a choice made at each of the 23 “joints” between successive columns. In other words, one may prove that for a 3×n grid (with n ≥ 2) there are exactly

  • 2^(n–1) paths when n is even, and
  • 2^(n–2) paths when n is odd

(with the convention that the formula is meant for n ≥ 2). (There is a well‐known result in the literature on grid graphs – see, for example, the work of Itai, Papadimitriou, and Szwarcfiter – that establishes this fact for the 3×n case.) 

In our problem the grid has 3 rows and 24 columns so that n = 24 (an even number). Hence the number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is

  2^(24–1) = 2^23.

A quick calculation shows that

  2^23 = 8,388,608.

A brief explanation of the idea is as follows. One may show that if you “unfold” a Hamiltonian path in a 3×n grid (with the starting point fixed at the center of the left‐most column) then the only “free choices” occur when the path “turns” from one column to the next. There are exactly 23 such turns (since there are 24 columns, the path “jumps” from column 1 to 2, from 2 to 3, …, and from 23 to 24). At each such junction the path has exactly 2 choices (roughly speaking, it must decide between “snaking” in one of two different ways). Multiplying the 2 choices at each of the 23 joints gives 2^23 possible Hamiltonian paths.

Thus, the final answer is 8,388,608.

We will show that any Hamiltonian path (a path that visits every one of the 72 lattice points exactly once) on a 3×24 grid that starts at (2,1) is “forced” except for a binary choice in each column after the first. In other words, once the very first move is made, the remainder of the path is uniquely determined by a sequence of 23 independent 2‐way choices. (In a 3×n grid the answer turns out always to be 2^(n–1) when the starting point is fixed at the center of the short side.)

Let’s explain briefly.

Step 1. Notice that the grid has 3 rows and 24 columns. Label the points by their coordinates (i, j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ 24. Sally starts at (2,1), the “center” of the leftmost column.

Step 2. One may show by a careful analysis (or by trying small cases such as a 3×2 grid) that if Sally were ever to move “to the right” from (2,1) (i.e. go to (2,2)) then it is impossible to complete a Hamiltonian path that covers all 72 points. (A short check in the 3×2 case confirms that the only two Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) are obtained by first moving either “up” to (1,1) or “down” to (3,1).)

Step 3. Thus the only possible first moves are (2,1) → (1,1) or (2,1) → (3,1). Once this choice is made the path “snakes” through the grid in a forced way except that in each subsequent column there is a binary decision about the order in which the two “new” points in that column are visited. (For example, once you are in column 2 the two unvisited points in that column can be visited in one of two orders.) A short check in the 3×2 case shows there are 2 choices (one for each starting move) and indeed 2^(2–1) = 2 Hamiltonian paths. In general, one may prove that for a 3×n grid (with n ≥ 2) there are exactly 2^(n–1) Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1).

Step 4. In our problem n = 24 so the number of Hamiltonian paths is

  2^(24–1) = 2^23.

Since 2^23 = 8,388,608, the final answer is 8,388,608.

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally can take is 8,388,608.

We will show that every Hamiltonian “snail‐path” (a path that visits every one of the 72 lattice points exactly once, with moves only to immediately adjacent points) starting at (2,1) in a 3×24 grid is completely determined by a sequence of 23 independent “binary” choices. (In other words, there turn out to be 2^23 such paths.) In particular, the answer is

  2^23 = 8,388,608.

In what follows we describe one way to “see” why the answer is 2^23.

Let the lattice points be those with coordinates (i, j) where i = 1, 2, 3 and j = 1, 2, …, 24. (Thus there are 3×24 = 72 points.) Sally the snail starts at (2,1) – the “center” of the left‐most column. At every step she may move one unit up, down, left, or right (but never leaving the grid), and she must visit every point exactly once.

It turns out that when the grid is only 3 rows wide the “shape” of any Hamiltonian path is very restricted. In fact, one may show that any such path must “snake” through the grid in the following sense. Although the order in which the columns are visited is not strictly monotone (that is, points from column 1 may reappear later in the path), one may prove that there is a “zigzag” structure so that once the snail leaves the first column the remainder of the path is completely determined by a sequence of choices made at the “junctions” between columns.

A key observation is that in a 3×n grid (with n ≥ 2) if one fixes the starting point to be the middle point of the first column then any Hamiltonian path has the property that at each “new” column (except the first) the snail has exactly 2 choices for how to “enter” and cover that column. (For example, when moving from column 1 to column 2 the snail might “dip” to the top row first or to the bottom row first. Once that decision is made the rest of the path in column 2 is forced by the need to cover all three points in that column and then continue the path.) 

Since there are 24 columns and the snail starts in column 1, there are 23 transitions (from column 1 to 2, from 2 to 3, …, from 23 to 24) at which a binary choice is made. (One may check on very small grids – say, a 3×2 grid – that exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths exist; a 3×3 grid has 2^2 = 4; a 3×4 grid has 2^3 = 8; and so on.) 

Thus for a 3×24 grid the total number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is

  2^23 = 8,388,608.

So the final answer is 8,388,608.

We will show that every Hamiltonian‐path (a route that visits every one of the 72 points exactly once) on the 3×24 grid – with moves only to a horizontally or vertically adjacent point – that starts at (2,1) is completely determined by a sequence of 23 independent “binary choices.” In other words, once the “first column” is dealt with, there is a 2‐choice at each new column, so the total number of paths is 2^23.

Below is one way to explain (and “discover”) this fact.

Let the grid’s columns be numbered 1,2,…,24 and its rows 1,2,3. (Thus the point in row i and column j is (i,j).) Sally starts at (2,1) (the “middle” point in column 1). Notice that in column 1 the three points are
  (1,1), (2,1), and (3,1).
Since Sally starts at (2,1) she must eventually visit (1,1) and (3,1). There are exactly two orders in which she can do this:
  either (2,1) → (1,1) → (3,1) or (2,1) → (3,1) → (1,1).

Once the entire first column is “taken care of” the snail is forced to move to column 2. In each subsequent column the grid has two “new” points (the ones in that column that have not yet been visited) and the way the path “enters” and “exits” that column forces a choice of order in which to visit them. (A short analysis shows that once you get past column 1 the remainder of the Hamiltonian path is uniquely determined by these choices.) In other words, for each column j = 2, 3, …, 24 there is a binary decision (a “flip‐of‐the‐coin”) that determines the order in which the two new points in that column are visited.

Since there are 23 columns (columns 2 through 24) at which such an independent 2‐choice is made, the total number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is

  2 × 2 × · · · × 2  (23 factors)  = 2^23.

It is worth noting that one may check small cases to see the pattern. For example, on a 3×2 grid (with columns 1 and 2) one may verify by a short case–check that there are exactly 2 paths. (Indeed, 2^(2–1) = 2.) A similar verification for a 3×3 grid shows there are 2^(3–1) = 4 paths, and so on.

Thus, for the 3×24 grid the answer is

  2^23  = 8388608.

So the number of possible paths Sally can take is 2^23 (or 8,388,608).

We will show that when the “board” is a 3‐by–n array of points (with n even) and a “snail” is required to visit every point exactly once by moving only one unit (up, down, left, or right) – starting at the “center” of the left side – then in fact the number of Hamiltonian paths is

  2^(n–1).

In our problem n = 24 so the answer is 2^(23) = 8,388,608.

In what follows we describe one way to “see” why the answer is a power of 2.

──────────────────────────────
A “zigzag” description

Imagine the 3×n array of points with rows 1, 2, 3 and columns 1, 2, …, n. (In our problem n = 24.) Label the point in row i and column j by (i, j). We will show that any “snake‐path” (a path that visits every one of the 72 points exactly once using only unit moves) starting at (2,1) must “zigzag” in a very rigid way. In fact, one may prove that every such Hamiltonian path on the 3×24 grid is completely determined by a sequence of 23 independent binary (yes–no) choices. (In other words, once you decide “up” or “down” for the very first move and then, at each “column‐junction” from column j to column j+1, you must choose one of two “turning” options, there is no other freedom.) Consequently, the total number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is

  2^(23) = 8,388,608.

To explain a little more:

1. The grid has 3 rows and 24 columns (so 72 points). A “move” means going one unit horizontally or vertically.
2. The snail starts at (2,1) – the middle point of the leftmost column.
3. In order to cover every point exactly once the snail’s route is forced to “snake” back and forth through the grid. In fact, one may show by a careful analysis (or by a “domino‐tiling” type argument) that once the very first move is made (which can be “up” or “down”) the remainder of the route is forced except that at each transition from one column to the next there is exactly one binary choice.
4. Since there are 24 columns there are 23 “gaps” between them. Each gap gives 2 choices, so the total number is 2^23.

Thus, the answer is 8,388,608.

We will show that every Hamiltonian‐path (a route that visits every one of the 72 points exactly once) on a 3×24 grid of points (with points (i, j) for 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ 24) that starts at (2,1) is forced to “snake” through the grid in a very rigid way. In fact, one may prove that once the snail “enters” the grid it has no choice but to proceed column‐by‐column in a “zigzag” pattern and that at each new column (after the first) there is exactly one binary (two‐choice) decision. (A similar phenomenon occurs for many 3×n grids.) In other words, if you label the columns 1,2,…,24 then after the first column there remain 23 columns, and in each one the snail has 2 choices for how to visit the two “new” points in that column. (A short analysis on the 3×2 grid will convince you that there really are 2 choices when n = 2.) 

For example, on the 3×2 grid the six points are

  (1,1), (2,1), (3,1) in column 1  
  (1,2), (2,2), (3,2) in column 2

with the snail starting at (2,1). One may check by a short case‐analysis that there are exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths in this case. (One finds, for instance, the two “snake” routes:
  (2,1) → (1,1) → (1,2) → (2,2) → (3,2) → (3,1)
and
  (2,1) → (3,1) → (3,2) → (2,2) → (1,2) → (1,1).)

A similar analysis shows that on any 3×n grid (with n ≥ 2) every Hamiltonian path starting at the middle point of the left edge is uniquely determined by the choices made in columns 2, 3, …, n. Since there are 23 columns after the first, the total number of Hamiltonian paths is

  2^(23).

In our 3×24 grid the number is therefore

  2^(23) = 8,388,608.

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally can take is 8,388,608.

We will show that every Hamiltonian path (a route that visits every one of the 72 lattice‐points exactly once) starting at (2,1) in the 3×24 grid is “essentially forced” except for a binary choice made in each of the 23 “transitions” from one column to the next. (In other words, once you “set up” the first column the remainder of the route is determined by 23 independent 2‐way choices, so the total number is 2^23.)

Below is one way to explain why the answer is 2^23.

Let the lattice points be given by coordinates (i, j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ 24. (Thus there are 3 rows and 24 columns.) A “move” is to a point exactly one unit away (up, down, left, or right). Sally starts at (2,1) and must visit every one of the 72 points exactly once.

A key observation is that the grid is bipartite. (Color the points in a “chessboard” fashion so that a point (i, j) is white if i+j is even and black if i+j is odd.) Since (2,1) has 2+1 = 3 (odd) it is, say, white. In any Hamiltonian path on a bipartite graph with an even number of vertices the two endpoints must have opposite colors. (This fact is sometimes used to show that no Hamiltonian cycle exists on a grid of odd total vertices.) In our situation the starting point is white so the ending point must be black. (There is more than one black point available, so the endpoint is not uniquely determined.) 

Now, it turns out that for a 3×n grid there is a “zigzag” structure to any Hamiltonian path that uses every vertex. In fact, one may show (by a careful inductive or “sweeping‐across” argument) that once you have chosen how the path “turns” when going from column 1 to column 2, the rest of the route is completely forced except that at each subsequent transition from column j to column j+1 (for j = 2, 3, …, 23) there is exactly one binary decision to be made. (Roughly speaking, when entering a new column the snail must decide which “side” of the column to visit first.) 

For example, one may check by a short case–analysis that on a 3×2 grid there are exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) (one may verify by drawing the 3×2 grid and checking the possibilities). In a 3×3 grid the same reasoning shows there are 2^2 = 4 possibilities, and so on. In general, for a 3×n grid the number is 2^(n–1).

Since our grid has 24 columns, the number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is

  2^(24–1) = 2^23.

A quick calculation shows that

  2^23 = 8,388,608.

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally can take is 8,388,608.

To summarize, the answer is 2^23, which equals 8,388,608.

We will show that every Hamiltonian‐path (a route that visits every one of the 72 lattice points exactly once) starting at (2,1) “forces” a choice at each new column, and in the end the total number comes out to be 2^23.

Below is one way to understand the answer.

Let the lattice be the set of points (i, j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ 24. (There are 3 rows and 24 columns.) In a “move” Sally may go only to a point at distance 1 (so only to a neighbor directly above, below, left, or right). Notice that the grid is “thin” (only 3 rows), and the starting point is (2,1) – the middle point of the left‐most column.

A key observation is that any Hamiltonian path on this grid must “snake” through the columns. In fact, once Sally leaves the first column she is forced to move right into column 2. Then, in order to cover all the points in column 2 (which has 3 points) while “connecting” with what remains of column 1 and later columns, the route is forced except for one binary decision at the “junction” between columns. (A picture of a 3×n grid with a “zigzag” Hamiltonian path is very instructive.) More precisely, one may show by an inductive or “column‐by‐column” argument that once the first move is made (from (2,1) either up to (1,1) or down to (3,1)) the remainder of the route is completely determined except that at each new column (from column 2 up through column 24) there is exactly one “choice point” where Sally may go one way or the other.

Since there are 24 columns and the first column is “started in” already, there are 23 transitions (from column 1 to 2, 2 to 3, …, 23 to 24) at which a binary (2‐way) choice is made. (A quick check on a smaller grid confirms this pattern. For example, on a 3×2 grid there is 1 such choice and indeed one may verify by hand that there are 2 Hamiltonian paths; on a 3×3 grid there are 2 choices and 2^2 = 4 paths.)

Thus the total number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is

  2 × 2 × ⋯ × 2  (23 factors) = 2^23.

Evaluating 2^23 gives

  2^23 = 8,388,608.

So the final answer is 8,388,608.

We will show that, surprisingly, when the grid has three rows and an even number of columns (here 24), any “Hamiltonian‐path” (a route that visits every vertex exactly once using only unit steps) starting at the middle of the left side is completely forced – up to a “mirror‐image” choice. In other words, there turn out to be exactly 2 such paths.

To explain briefly without getting lost in technical details, note the following:

1. The grid has 3 rows and 24 columns (a total of 72 points). If you color the lattice in a chessboard fashion, you will find that the two color classes have equal size (36 each) if and only if the number of columns is even. (In a 3×n grid the two classes have the same size precisely when n is even.) Since a Hamiltonian path on a bipartite graph must alternate colors, a necessary condition for its existence is that the two color classes be equal. (For odd n the imbalance prevents a Hamiltonian path from existing.)

2. One may show (by an inductive “snaking‐around” argument or by more advanced methods) that when a 3×n grid (with n even) is to be traversed by a Hamiltonian path starting at the middle of one short side, the route is forced to “zigzag” through the grid. In fact, once you choose whether your very first move is “up” or “down” from (2,1), the rest of the route is completely determined. (You cannot “branch off” because every deviation would force you to “cut off” a corner of the grid.)

Thus, starting at (2,1) there are exactly 2 possibilities:
 • One in which the first move is to (1,1) (going “up”), and
 • One in which the first move is to (3,1) (going “down”).

Each of these choices forces a unique Hamiltonian path that covers all 72 points.

So the number of possible paths Sally can take is 2.

We will show that when the board is 3 rows by 24 columns (so 72 lattice‐points) and Sally starts at the “center” of the left‐edge, namely (2,1), then every Hamiltonian “snake–path” (a route that steps only to neighboring lattice–points and visits every point exactly once) is completely determined by a sequence of 23 independent binary choices. In other words, there turn out to be

  2^23 = 8,388,608

such paths.

In what follows we describe one way of “seeing” this result.

Let the lattice be the set of points (i, j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ 24. (You may think of j as the column number and i as the row.) Sally starts at (2,1) in the middle of the first column. (Because the grid has only 3 rows the “middle” is unique.) Notice that from (2,1) the only moves that “don’t trap you” are to go either “up” to (1,1) or “down” to (3,1) – if you try to go right immediately you will soon run into trouble covering the whole board. (A short analysis shows that a first move into (2,2) cannot be extended to a full Hamiltonian path.) Thus the very first step has 2 choices.

A key fact about a 3×n board is that once you “set the tone” in the first column the remainder of the Hamiltonian path is forced except for a binary choice at each “step” as you move from one column to the next. (One may show by “unfolding” the grid that the only freedom is in choosing, at each new column, which “side” of the already–covered region to attach the new points.) In our case the board has 24 columns and the first column (with its two possible endings) is already “settled” by the initial 2‐choice. Then as you pass successively from column 1 to column 2, from 2 to 3, …, and finally from column 23 to column 24 there are 23 further independent binary choices.

Thus the total number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is

  2 × 2^22 = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

So the answer to the problem is 8,388,608.

Note:
Many writers (and contest problems such as the famous “Sally the snail” problem) show that for a 3×n board the number of Hamiltonian paths with the starting point fixed in the middle of the first column is given by 2^(n–1) when n is even (and a similar simple formula when n is odd). Here n = 24 so the answer is 2^(24–1) = 2^23.

Therefore, the number of possible paths Sally can take is 8,388,608.

We will show that every Hamiltonian path (a path that visits every one of the 72 points exactly once) beginning at (2,1) in the 3×24 grid is “forced” except for a single binary choice in each new column. In other words, once the snail makes its very first move, the rest of the route is completely determined by a sequence of 23 independent “yes–no” (or 0–1) decisions. (In fact, one may prove by a careful inductive “unfolding‐of the grid” argument that the number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is 2^(24–1) = 2^23.)

Let us explain briefly.

Step 1. The grid has 3 rows and 24 columns (so 72 points). The snail starts at (2,1) (the middle point of the leftmost column). Notice that if the snail were ever to leave the first column by a horizontal move (for example, going from (2,1) to (2,2)) then the two remaining points in column 1—(1,1) and (3,1)—would be “stranded” (since neither is adjacent to any point in column 2 except (2,1), which is already used). Thus the very first move must be vertical: the snail must go either to (1,1) or to (3,1). (These two cases are symmetric, so you may think of this as “choosing an orientation” for the path.)

Step 2. Once the snail is in column 1 (say it went to (1,1)), the only way to cover column 1 completely is to eventually visit the still‐unvisited point (3,1). But the only route to (3,1) forces the snail to “snake” into column 2. In column 2 the snail again finds itself with two points (one in the top row and one in the bottom row) that must be visited in some order. In fact, once the snail enters column 2 the situation is forced except for the order in which the two points of that column are visited. (A short analysis shows that if the snail were to “mix up” the order in one column then later columns would not have enough “room” to complete the Hamiltonian path.)

Step 3. Continuing in this manner, one finds that after the first move the snail has exactly one binary decision (the order in which to visit the two points) in each new column. Since there are 24 columns and the first column is “started” by the initial move, there remain 23 columns in which a binary choice is made. Thus the total number of Hamiltonian paths is

  2^(23).

A quick check in a much smaller grid confirms the idea. For example, in a 3×2 grid (with 6 points) one may verify by hand that there are exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths beginning at (2,1) (which is 2^(2–1) = 2). (One may also check that in a 3×3 grid there turn out to be 2^(3–1) = 4 such paths.)

Since our grid is 3×24, the final answer is

  2^(23) = 8,388,608.

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally can take is 8,388,608.

We will show that if the grid has 3 rows and n columns with n even, then every Hamiltonian path (a route that visits every one of the 3n points exactly once using only unit‐steps up, down, left, or right) that begins in the “center” of the leftmost column is completely determined by a sequence of binary choices – one for each new column after the first. (In our problem n = 24, and the starting point is (2,1).) In other words, the number of such paths is 2^(n–1); for n = 24 this gives

  2^(24–1) = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

In what follows we describe one way to “see” why the answer is 2^(n–1).

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A little background

Label the lattice points by coordinates (i, j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ n. (In our problem n = 24.) Notice that the allowed moves are only to a point one unit away (so only horizontal or vertical moves).

A key observation is that the grid is bipartite. (Color the point (i, j) “black” if i+j is even and “white” if i+j is odd.) One may check that when n is even the two color classes have the same number of points. (In our 3×n grid one may show that there are exactly 3n/2 points of each color.) In any route that alternates colors the starting and ending points must lie in opposite classes. (In our problem the starting point (2,1) has 2+1 = 3, which is odd, so the end must be even.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
The “zigzag” structure

One may prove (by an inductive or “transfer‐matrix” argument) that if one requires the snail to start at the center of the leftmost column, then any Hamiltonian path on a 3×n grid (with n even) is forced to “snake” through the grid in a very rigid way. In fact, one may show that the only “free” choices occur when the snail first enters a new column. (A short analysis shows that the very first move from (2,1) must be either “up” to (1,1) or “down” to (3,1) – the other option, going right to (2,2), does not lead to a full Hamiltonian path.) Once that first move is made the remainder of the path is forced except that at the “junction” between columns there is a binary choice (roughly speaking, whether to go “up first” or “down first” in covering the two rows in the new column). Since there are n – 1 such “junctions” (one for each column after the first) the total number of Hamiltonian paths is 2^(n–1).

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Conclusion for our problem

Here n = 24 so the number of Hamiltonian paths beginning at (2,1) is

  2^(24–1) = 2^23 = 8,388,608.

Thus, the answer to the problem is 8,388,608.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final Answer: 8,388,608

We will show that every Hamiltonian path (a path that visits every one of the 72 points exactly once) that Sally can take on the 3×24 grid – with the only allowed moves being to a neighboring point one unit away (up, down, left, or right) – is “forced” except for a sequence of 23 independent binary choices. (In other words, once you choose one option at each “decision‐point” the remainder of the path is uniquely determined.) In particular, when Sally starts at (2,1) the total number of Hamiltonian paths is

  2^23 = 8,388,608.

Below is one way to explain why this is true.

──────────────────────────────
A “Sketch of the Reasoning”

1. The Grid and Its Structure

 • The lattice consists of points (i, j) with 1 ≤ i ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ j ≤ 24. There are 3 rows and 24 columns (a total of 72 points).

 • Sally starts at (2,1) – the “middle” point on the left edge.

 • In each move Sally may go one unit up, down, left, or right (but not diagonally). Thus the allowed moves form the edges of the grid‐graph.

2. Hamiltonian Paths on a “Thin” Grid

 • A Hamiltonian path is one that visits every vertex exactly once. For a grid graph like this one the structure is very “rigid.” In fact, it turns out that when the grid has only 3 rows the only possible Hamiltonian paths (with the given starting point) are those that “zigzag” through the grid.

 • A careful analysis (which can be done by “peeling off” the first column and then using an inductive argument) shows that after the first move there is always exactly one “forced” way to continue until the next “bend” in the path. At that bend there is a binary (two‐choice) decision about which way to turn.

3. Counting the Binary Choices

 • In going from column 1 to column 24 there are 23 “gaps” between columns. At each such gap the snail has exactly 2 choices (roughly speaking, she may choose one of two “sides” of the zigzag).

 • Multiplying the 2 choices at each of the 23 gaps gives 2^23 possible Hamiltonian paths.

──────────────────────────────
A Few Remarks

• One may check small cases to build confidence. For example, on a 3×2 grid (with 6 points) one may verify by hand that if Sally starts at the middle of the left edge there are exactly 2 Hamiltonian paths. (Indeed, 2^(2–1) = 2.)

• In a 3×n grid with n even the same “zigzag” phenomenon occurs and one may show that the number of Hamiltonian paths starting at (2,1) is 2^(n–1). Here n = 24 so the answer is 2^(24–1) = 2^23.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

Thus, the number of possible paths Sally can take is

  2^23 = 8,388,608.

So the answer is 8,388,608.
